title: Tamburlaine the Great, Part 1
description: Marlowe's first play and the manifesto of Elizabethan blank verse drama: the Scythian shepherd Tamburlaine rises by conquest to overthrow kings, takes the Egyptian princess Zenocrate, defeats the Persian Cosroe, and tramples the Turkish emperor Bajazeth in his cage — the play closing with Tamburlaine's marriage and his vow of further conquests, 'still climbing after knowledge infinite'.
plot_or_argument: Tamburlaine, armed with eloquence and terror, wins Zenocrate, deposes Mycetes, and crowns himself after Cosroe's fall; Bajazeth and Zabina are caged and mocked; Damascus is sacked for its defiance, Zenocrate's father pardoned for her sake; the play ends with the betrothal and the tyrant's speech of unappeasable aspiration.
narrative_structure: A two-part rise structured as a chain of conquests and debates, with the great set speeches — 'Is it not passing brave to be a king' — as its pillars.
principal_characters: Tamburlaine; Zenocrate; Bajazeth; Zabina; Mycetes; Cosroe; Theridamas; Techelles; Usumcasane; Agydas; the Soldan of Egypt
meter_and_prosody: The 'mighty line' — Marlowe's blank verse of sweeping hyperbole and classical allusion, which transformed the English stage.
historical_context: Performed by the Admiral's Men in 1587, the Armada year; its prologue's defiance of 'jigging veins of rhyming mother-wits' announced the new poetics that Shakespeare's generation inherited.
literary_significance: The first great English blank-verse tragedy and the fountainhead of Elizabethan heroic drama; its hero became the type of the Renaissance overreacher.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Jones, 1590. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Frank Romany and Robert Lindsey (Penguin, 2003).

title: Tamburlaine the Great, Part 2
description: The sequel Marlowe was pressed to write after Part 1's success: Tamburlaine's further conquests — the slaughter of the virgins of Damascus, the bridling of the conquered kings who draw his chariot, his burning of the Koran at Babylon — until the death of Zenocrate breaks him, his own sickness follows, and the 'scourge of God' dies in his camp, his empire uncompleted.
plot_or_argument: Tamburlaine defeats the Christian Sigismund's treachery, kills his coward son Calyphas, humbles the Turkish and Egyptian powers, and burns the Koran in defiance; Zenocrate's death opens the way to his own — the physician's verdict, the self-anatomy in the mirror, and the dying survey of the map of the world he could not finish conquering.
narrative_structure: A series of conquests and defiances culminating in the two deaths, with the chariot scene and the burning of the books as the peaks of its provocation.
principal_characters: Tamburlaine; Zenocrate; Calyphas; Amyras; Celebinus; Orcanes; Sigismund; Callapine; the Turkish Concubines; the Physician
meter_and_prosody: The mighty line at its most sustained, with the dying speeches of Zenocrate and Tamburlaine as its elegiac close.
historical_context: Written immediately after Part 1 and printed with it in 1590; its burnings and blasphemies made Marlowe's name feared as well as famous.
literary_significance: The completion of the first great two-part epic of the English stage and the template for the overreacher's fall.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Richard Jones, 1590. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Frank Romany and Robert Lindsey (Penguin, 2003).

title: Doctor Faustus
alternative_titles: The Tragical History of the Life and Death of Doctor Faustus
description: Marlowe's tragedy of the scholar who sells his soul: Wittenberg's Faustus, sated with all knowledge, signs away his soul to Lucifer for twenty-four years of Mephistopheles' service — and spends them on empty marvels, pageants of the seven deadly sins, and the phantom Helen, whose kiss is the play's summit ('the face that launched a thousand ships') — until the last hour's soliloquy and the devils' claim.
plot_or_argument: Faustus conjures Mephistopheles, signs the bond in blood, and debates theology with the demon; the good and evil angels contend for him through the middle acts of farce and magic; his repentance is always deferred — 'I'll burn my books' never said in time — and the midnight soliloquy ends with the Scholars finding his 'mangled limbs'.
narrative_structure: A morality play inverted: the psychomachy of the angels, the pageant of sins, and the Old Man's pleas all fail against the irreversible bond, in a structure whose comic middle scenes are partly the work of collaborators.
principal_characters: Doctor Faustus; Mephistopheles; Wagner; Lucifer; the Good Angel; the Evil Angel; the Old Man; Valdes; Cornelius; the Horse-Courser; Robin; Rafe; Helen of Troy; the Scholars
meter_and_prosody: The mighty line at its most lyrical — the apostrophe to Helen and the final soliloquy are the touchstones of Elizabethan blank verse.
historical_context: Based on the German Faustbuch in its English translation (c. 1592); the play exists in two texts (the A-text of 1604 and the expanded B-text of 1616), and its conjuring scenes were blamed for real devils in the audience.
literary_significance: The founding myth of modern damnation drama — the play that gave Goethe, and the world, the figure of Faust.
attribution_notes: Marlowe's authorship of the core is uncontested; the comic scenes include the hand of collaborators (probably Samuel Rowley and William Bird).
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1604 (A-text); Quarto, 1616 (B-text). Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Frank Romany and Robert Lindsey (Penguin, 2003).

title: The Jew of Malta
description: Marlowe's black comedy of Machiavellian revenge: the merchant Barabas, his wealth seized to pay Malta's tribute to the Turks, revenges himself on the Christian state by intrigue and poison, betrays the island to the Turks, and is finally caught in his own engine — the cauldron prepared for his enemies — in a play whose prologue is spoken by 'Machevill' himself.
plot_or_argument: Barabas is stripped of his estate; through his daughter Abigail he recovers his hidden gold and buys the deaths of the governor's son and suitor; Abigail's conversion and death, his purchase of the slave Ithamore, and the double poisonings follow; made governor by the Turks, he plots the city's destruction, but the falling floor delivers him to the cauldron and the Christians' triumph.
narrative_structure: A five-act intrigue of escalating double-dealing, alternating the prologue's sardonic commentary with farcical villainy, and ending in the spectacular engine of the cauldron.
principal_characters: Barabas; Abigail; Ithamore; Ferneze, governor of Malta; Lodowick; Mathias; Calymath; Bellamira; Pilia-Borza; the two Friars (Jacomo and Bernardine); Machevill (the Prologue)
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse for Barabas's great soliloquies of gold ('infinite riches in a little room') against the prose of the play's farcical intrigues.
historical_context: Performed from 1592, in the aftermath of the Lopez affair and the Marrano anxieties of the 1590s; not printed until 1633, when it was revived with prologues by Heywood.
literary_significance: The most corrosive of the Elizabethan revenge plays — a satire of Christian, Jew, and Turk alike that Shakespeare answered in Shylock.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1633. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Frank Romany and Robert Lindsey (Penguin, 2003).

title: Edward II
alternative_titles: The Troublesome Reign and Lamentable Death of Edward the Second
description: Marlowe's history play of a king undone by favouritism: Edward's dotage on Gaveston and then on the Spensers alienates his queen Isabella and the barons; rebellion, deposition, and the murder at Berkeley Castle follow — the famous stage direction of Lightborn's red-hot spit — in the first great English tragedy of state and private passion.
plot_or_argument: Edward recalls Gaveston from exile; the barons capture and kill him; the king's grief turns to the Spensers and to revenge on Lancaster and Warwick; Isabella and Mortimer invade, the favourites fall, and Edward is deposed, imprisoned, and murdered by Lightborn, while the play ends with young Edward III's execution of Mortimer and the lament over his father's bier.
narrative_structure: A chronicle tragedy of rise, fall, and retribution in the de casibus pattern, notable for the equal weight given to the king's grief and the barons' politics.
principal_characters: King Edward II; Gaveston; Queen Isabella; Mortimer the younger; the Earl of Lancaster; the Earl of Warwick; the Spensers (father and son); Edmund of Woodstock, Earl of Kent; Lightborn; Prince Edward (Edward III)
meter_and_prosody: A blank verse newly capable of the political and the intimate — the abdication scene and the prison soliloquy are its heights — which taught Shakespeare the form of Richard II.
historical_context: Written about 1592 from Holinshed; printed 1594; its deposition scenes and its treatment of favouritism and sodomy made it the riskiest of the chronicle plays.
literary_significance: The first fully achieved English history tragedy of psychology and state, and the direct model for Shakespeare's second tetralogy.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1594. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Frank Romany and Robert Lindsey (Penguin, 2003).

title: The Massacre at Paris
description: Marlowe's late topical tragedy of the St Bartholomew's Day massacre (1572): the Duke of Guise, with the Queen Mother Catherine de Medici, engineers the slaughter of the Huguenots; the Protestant hero Ramus dies; and the play runs through the assassinations of Guise and of Henry III to the accession of the Protestant Henry of Navarre.
plot_or_argument: Guise murders the Huguenot leadership and the scholar Ramus; Navarre escapes the massacre; the Guise's ambition threatens the crown itself until Henry III has him killed; the friar's dagger avenges Guise by killing the king, and the play ends with Navarre's triumph and England's alliance.
narrative_structure: A compressed chronicle of murder and counter-murder — the surviving text (an octavo of about 1,250 lines) is clearly a cut or memorially reconstructed version of a longer play.
principal_characters: the Duke of Guise; Catherine de Medici; Henry III of France; Henry of Navarre; Ramus; the Duke of Anjou; the Cardinal of Lorraine; Mugeroun; the Friar
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse with the 'mighty line' audible in the surviving fragments, notably Guise's soliloquies of ambition.
historical_context: Performed by Strange's Men in January 1593, in the wake of Henri IV's conversion and English fears of the Catholic League; printed in a poor octavo about 1594.
literary_significance: The first English play of contemporary European politics — Protestant propaganda raised to tragedy, surviving only in mutilated form.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the text is evidently a damaged report of the original.
bibliographical_notes: Undated octavo, c. 1594. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Frank Romany and Robert Lindsey (Penguin, 2003).

title: Dido, Queen of Carthage
description: Marlowe's earliest surviving play, written with Thomas Nashe, from Virgil's Aeneid: Aeneas, shipwrecked at Carthage, tells Dido the tale of Troy's fall; she loves him, he is commanded away by Jove, and her suicide on the pyre ends the play — a tragedy of love's rhetoric and the gods' indifference, performed by the Children of the Chapel.
plot_or_argument: Venus disguises herself to guide Aeneas ashore; the courtship in the cave, the rivalry with Iarbas, and the recital of Priam's fall fill the middle acts; the false Ascanius (Cupid) kindles Dido's passion; the gods recall Aeneas; and Dido, abandoned, mounts the pyre with his gifts and dies cursing him.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragedy for boy players, structured on the Virgilian books I–IV, with the great set piece of Aeneas's narration of Troy at its centre.
principal_characters: Dido; Aeneas; Anna; Iarbas; Achates; Venus; Juno; Jupiter; Cupid (as Ascanius); the Nurse
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of a chamber-music delicacy suited to the children's company, with the speeches of Dido's grief as its lyric summit.
historical_context: Probably written at Cambridge in the mid-1580s and revised for the Children of the Chapel; printed in 1594 with both names on the title page.
literary_significance: The seed of English classical tragedy — Marlowe's and Nashe's schoolroom Virgil become a stage poem of love and abandonment.
attribution_notes: Title page assigns the play to Marlowe and Nashe jointly; the division of scenes is uncertain.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1594. Standard edition: The Complete Plays of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Frank Romany and Robert Lindsey (Penguin, 2003).

title: Hero and Leander
description: Marlowe's unfinished Ovidian epyllion, left at the lovers' first night and completed by George Chapman in 1598: the priestess Hero of Sestos and the youth Leander of Abydos meet at Venus's festival and fall in love; Leander swims the Hellespont nightly, and the poem breaks off with the consummation — 'Love is not full of pity, as men say' — before Hero's death in the familiar myth.
plot_or_argument: Leander, 'amorous Leander, beautiful and young', woos Hero at the feast of Adonis; her vows to Venus yield to his eloquence; the first swim, the first embrace, and the lovers' debate with the dawn occupy the completed portion, with Neptune's dalliance with the swimming Leander as its most celebrated episode.
narrative_structure: Two completed sestiads (Marlowe's) followed by Chapman's four, the whole framed as a narrative of seduction and delay in the epyllion manner.
principal_characters: Hero; Leander; Neptune; Venus; Cupid; the Nurse (Chapman's continuation)
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of extraordinary wit and sensuousness — the poem that defined the English erotic couplet for the next two centuries.
historical_context: Written in 1593, the year of Marlowe's death; printed first by Edward Blount in 1598 and again the same year with Chapman's continuation ('Hero and Leander: Begun by Christopher Marloe; and finished by George Chapman').
literary_significance: The masterpiece of the Elizabethan epyllion and the direct ancestor of the Restoration erotic couplet — the poem Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis answered and vied with.
attribution_notes: Marlowe's two sestiads are uncontested; the continuation is Chapman's.
bibliographical_notes: Printed by Edward Blount, 1598. Standard edition: The Complete Poems and Translations of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Stephen Orgel (Penguin, 1971).

title: All Ovid's Elegies
description: Marlowe's translation of Ovid's Amores into English heroic couplets — the first complete English version of the Roman love elegies, in which the poet-lover's campaigns in the bedroom, his mistress Corinna, and the whole erotic repertoire of Augustan Rome are rendered with Marlowe's characteristic audacity; the book was condemned and burned by the bishops' ban of 1599.
plot_or_argument: The three books of the Amores move through the lover's slavery to Corinna, the rivalries, quarrels, and reconciliations of the affair, the impotence elegy, and the final renunciation of love elegy for tragedy — each poem an erotic set piece in the Ovidian manner.
narrative_structure: A sequence of some forty-eight elegies in three books, translated in order from the Amores, with Marlowe's ten elegies to a serving-wench translating Ovid with his usual freedom.
principal_characters: the poet-lover; Corinna; the eunuch Bagoas; the bawd Dipsas; Aurora
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets — Marlowe's chosen form for Ovid's elegiacs — of a frankness that scandalized the authorities.
historical_context: Printed surreptitiously in the late 1590s and burned under the Bishops' Ban of 1599 along with the satires of Marston and Hall; all early editions survive only in fragments.
literary_significance: The first full English Ovid of the Renaissance erotic tradition — the text that made Marlowe's name a byword for atheism and licence, and a model for Donne's elegies.
bibliographical_notes: Printed at Middleburgh, c. 1599 (all copies mutilated or burned). Standard edition: The Complete Poems and Translations of Christopher Marlowe, ed. Stephen Orgel (Penguin, 1971).

title: Every Man in His Humour
description: Jonson's first great comedy of humours, performed by the Lord Chamberlain's Men with Shakespeare in the cast: the jealous merchant Kitely, the braggart Captain Bobadill, the town gull Matthew, and the poetaster's crew are all 'humorous' — each ruled by an obsession — until the exposure of the final act lets the sane (Clement, Wellbred) judge the fools, in a London whose names Jonson later anglicized from the Italian setting.
plot_or_argument: Old Knowell worries over his son's London dissipations; Kitely suspects his wife; Bobadill boasts and fights by words only; the gulls and their plots collide at Cob's house, and Justice Clement's court of the final scene administers the comic verdicts — including the purging of the humours by the 'vent' of exposure.
narrative_structure: A unified-plot comedy on the classical model — one city, one day, one action — built on the humours theory announced in the Induction and resolved in the judgment scene.
principal_characters: Kitely; Dame Kitely; Captain Bobadill; Edward Knowell; Brainworm; Wellbred; Stephen; Matthew; Justice Clement; Downright; Bridget; Cob; Tib
meter_and_prosody: Mostly prose in the 1616 Folio revision, with the verse of the earlier Italian version smoothed away — the first great prose comedy of the English stage.
historical_context: Performed 1598 at the Curtain by the Chamberlain's Men (Shakespeare played Old Knowell); Jonson revised the play, resetting it in London, for the 1616 Folio of his Works.
literary_significance: The foundation of Jonson's comic method and of the English comedy of character — the template for Restoration and eighteenth-century comedy alike.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1601 (Italian setting); revised text in the Folio, 1616. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: Volpone
description: Jonson's greatest comedy, a beast fable of greed: the magnifico Volpone, the Fox, feigns death to draw gifts from the legacy hunters Voltore (the vulture), Corbaccio (the raven), and Corvino (the crow); with his parasite Mosca, the Fly, he escalates the game to Corvino's offer of his own wife Celia — until the dupes, double-crossed, drag the plot into the Venetian courts and the final, ferocious sentences.
plot_or_argument: The suitors heap gold on the 'dying' Volpone; Corbaccio disinherits his son, Corvino prostitutes Celia; Volpone's attempted rape of Celia is exposed in the trial scenes, where Mosca's perjury and Volpone's disguises nearly win; the trickster's final mock-death turns Mosca to his own advantage, and the double betrayal brings everything before the Avocatori, who strip, sentence, and exile them all.
narrative_structure: A five-act intrigue in the classical manner, with the sub-plot of Sir Politic Would-Be's English follies (a Lady Would-be's parrot) as satirical counterpoint, and the mountebank scene as its comic summit.
principal_characters: Volpone; Mosca; Voltore; Corbaccio; Corvino; Celia; Bonario; Sir Politic Would-Be; Lady Would-Be; Peregrine; Nano; Castrone; Androgyno; the Avocatori
meter_and_prosody: Blank verse of a muscular, satirical energy, with the mountebank's prose sales pitch and the songs of the deformed fools.
historical_context: Performed at the Globe and both universities in 1606; its Venice is a mirror of Jacobean London's gold-rush, and its Epistle and prologue announce Jonson's classical ambitions.
literary_significance: The most perfectly constructed comedy in English — a moral anatomy of greed that has never lost its bite.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1607; Folio, 1616. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: Epicene
description: Jonson's comedy of noise and silence: Morose, who cannot bear sound, marries the 'silent woman' Epicene to disinherit his nephew Dauphine — only to find his bride a torrent of talk, his house invaded by the collegiate ladies and the barber Cutbeard, and the play's last trick the revelation that Epicene is a boy, Dauphine's instrument, and the marriage void.
plot_or_argument: Dauphine plots to break his uncle's will: the silent bride, the mock divorce consultation, and the siege of Morose's house by the Otiers' collegiates drive the old man to any terms; the contract signed, Dauphine strips the boy of his disguise and the play ends on the audience's own exposure to satire.
narrative_structure: A five-act farce of escalating noise and counter-plot, with the collegiate ladies' scenes as a satire of female learning and the divorce farce as its centrepiece.
principal_characters: Morose; Dauphine; Epicene; Truewit; Clerimont; Sir John Daw; Sir Amorous La Foole; Captain Otter; Mistress Otter; Cutbeard; Mavis; the collegiates
meter_and_prosody: Predominantly prose — Jonson's most assured comic prose — with the wit-duels of Truewit as its set pieces.
historical_context: First performed by the Children of the Queen's Revels at Whitefriars, 1609; its boy-bride was played by a boy, doubling the play's game with gender; printed in the 1616 Folio.
literary_significance: The most audacious of Jonson's comedies of sex and gender — the play Restoration comedy learned its tricks from.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the Folio, 1616. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: The Alchemist
description: Jonson's comedy of alchemical confidence tricks: in Lovewit's vacated London house during the plague, Subtle the alchemist, Face the housekeeper, and Doll Common the prostitute run their roaring shop, fleecing the knight Sir Epicure Mammon, the tobacconist Abel Drugger, the Puritan brethren Ananias and Tribulation, and the quarrelling Kastril — until Lovewit's return and the final distribution of the spoils.
plot_or_argument: Each gull arrives with a different dream — the philosopher's stone for Mammon, a lucky shop for Drugger, the widow Pliant for Kastril, the orphans' goods for the Puritans — and each is worked by the 'venture tripartite' of Subtle, Face, and Doll; the quarrels of the conspirators and the return of the master bring the whole house of cards down in the last act's cascade of exposures.
narrative_structure: A single-day, single-house intrigue observing the classical unities to the letter, with each act a fresh round of gulling and the final act a tournament of unmaskings.
principal_characters: Subtle; Face (Jeremy); Doll Common; Sir Epicure Mammon; Surly; Abel Drugger; Ananias; Tribulation Wholesome; Kastril; Dame Pliant; Lovewit; the Neighbours
meter_and_prosody: Verse for the gulls' fantastic speeches (Mammon's visions of the stone), prose for the roaring shop's business — Jonson's richest mix.
historical_context: Performed by the King's Men in 1610 and printed in 1612; its plague setting mirrored the London closures of 1609–10, and its Puritans were recognized at once.
literary_significance: Generally reckoned the greatest English comedy after Shakespeare — the most perfect machine of comic construction in the language.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1612; Folio, 1616. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: Bartholomew Fair
description: Jonson's comedy of the fair: on St Bartholomew's Day, the whole of London pours into Smithfield — the justice Adam Overdo in disguise, the hot Puritan Zeal-of-the-Land Busy, the gallants Winwife and Quarlous, the pig-woman Ursula and her booth, the puppet-show of Hero and Leander — in a play whose carnival world exposes every pretension, and whose induction mocks its own audience's 'warrant' for the satire.
plot_or_argument: Overdo patrols the fair to 'enormities' in disguise; Busy denounces the fleshpots and falls to the pig; the gallants win the rich widow and the ward through the fair's games; the cutpurse Edgeworth and the bawd Whit ply their trades; and the last act's puppet trial before Overdo ends with the puppets' own argument and the universal pardon of the fair.
narrative_structure: A deliberately sprawling carnival structure — no single plot, but a cross-section of the fair in five acts, with Overdo's exposures as the running joke and the puppet trial as the finale.
principal_characters: Adam Overdo; Dame Overdo; Zeal-of-the-Land Busy; Winwife; Quarlous; Bartholomew Cokes; Grace Wellborn; Wasp; Ursula the pig-woman; Leatherhead (Lantern); Joan Trash; Edgeworth; Whit; Justice Trouble-All; the Puppets
meter_and_prosody: Almost wholly prose — the most populous and idiomatic prose of Jonson's career — with the puppets' verse as the final parody.
historical_context: First performed at the Hope theatre on 31 October 1614, before James I; printed 1631; its 'enormities' satire answers the puritan attacks on the stage Jonson had answered in his own person.
literary_significance: The greatest carnival play in English — a comedy that swallows its own satire and leaves the audience judged along with the fair.
bibliographical_notes: First printed 1631 (from the 1614 performance). Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: Sejanus His Fall
description: Jonson's Roman tragedy of the favourite's fall: the ambitious Sejanus, minister of Tiberius, destroys the house of Germanicus piece by piece and rises toward the throne itself — until Tiberius's letter from Capri, read in the Senate, turns the city against him, and the mob tears him to pieces in the streets, his children executed, his statues melted down.
plot_or_argument: Sejanus corrupts and removes Drusus, Agrippina, and their sons; the senators' servility and the informers' trade fill the middle acts; the emperor's withdrawal and the counter-plot of Macro prepare the fall; the Senate scene reverses Sejanus's fortunes in a single letter, and the final act follows the executioners through the city's vengeance.
narrative_structure: A five-act tragedy of state built on Tacitus, with the Senate scenes as its rhetorical engine and the messenger's report of the mob's savagery as its climax.
principal_characters: Sejanus; Tiberius; Macro; Silius; Arruntius; Agrippina; Drusus; Livia; the Senate; Cordus; Natta; Eudemus
meter_and_prosody: A grave, scholarly blank verse with extensive marginal annotation in the printed text — the play as documented history.
historical_context: Performed at the Globe in 1603 (with Shakespeare in the cast), then revised for print in 1605, with Jonson's marginal notes citing his classical authorities; it landed him before the Privy Council on charges of 'popery and treason'.
literary_significance: The first great English political tragedy of the Jacobean age and the founding text of the Roman play's documentary tradition.
attribution_notes: Uncontested, though the original Globe version contained a share by another hand, which Jonson replaced for the printed text.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1605; Folio, 1616. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: The Masque of Blackness
description: The first of Jonson's great court masques, designed by Inigo Jones and danced by Queen Anne and her ladies: twelve nymphs of Niger, blackened by the sun, voyage to 'Britannia' in a giant sea-shell seeking the land whose sun (King James) can whiten them — the masque of racial transformation that founded the Stuart court's most spectacular genre.
plot_or_argument: Niger, his daughters, and the moon-goddess Aethiopia arrive in a moving shell drawn by sea-monsters; the songs announce that the nymphs must seek 'a land whose name is Britannia'; they dance, and the final song promises their cleansing by the British sun — a transformation deferred to the sequel, The Masque of Beauty (1608).
narrative_structure: A single masque of arrival and prophecy — antimasque, main masque, and revels — with Jones's machinery (the moving shell, the painted waves) as equal partner to Jonson's verse.
principal_characters: Niger; Aethiopia; the twelve nymphs (danced by Queen Anne and her ladies); Oceanus
meter_and_prosody: Songs in varied lyric forms with the speeches in blank verse, the whole scaled to the banqueting house's acoustics and spectacle.
historical_context: Performed at Whitehall on Twelfth Night, 6 January 1605, with the Queen herself blackened in body-paint; the masque's racial and political meanings — union, empire, and whiteness — are now the subject of intense critical debate.
literary_significance: The inauguration of the Jonson–Jones masque, the Stuart court's supreme art form, and a text now central to studies of race in the Renaissance.
attribution_notes: Uncontested; the setting and machines are Inigo Jones's designs.
bibliographical_notes: Quarto, 1608. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: Epigrams
description: Jonson's collection of 133 epigrams, printed in the 1616 Folio of his Works: poems of praise to the great and good of his acquaintance (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; the Sidneys; Donne; Shakespeare), and poems of satiric castigation to the vicious — 'On Court-Worm', 'On Gut', 'On My First Son', and the epitaphs on his children among them — the classical epigram remade as a moral instrument.
plot_or_argument: No plot: the collection alternates poems of praise and blame, with the commendatory poems to patrons and fellow poets balancing the satires of fools and knaves, and the personal elegies (on his son, on his first daughter) at the collection's heart.
narrative_structure: A book of 133 short poems in the Martial tradition, arranged as a gallery of virtues and vices, prefaced by Jonson's defence of the genre.
principal_characters: the poet; the named patrons and poets (Lucy, Countess of Bedford; Donne; Shakespeare; the Sidneys); the satirized types (Court-Worm, Gut, Poet-Ape)
meter_and_prosody: Heroic couplets of lapidary finish — the model for the Augustan couplet of the next century.
historical_context: Written across Jonson's career and collected for the 1616 Works, the first folio of an English playwright's own canon; 'To the Memory of My Beloved, the Author, Mr. William Shakespeare' appeared separately in the 1623 Folio.
literary_significance: The foundation of the English epigram tradition and the seedbed of the Augustan moral couplet.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the Folio, 1616. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).

title: The Forest
description: Jonson's collection of fifteen poems printed in the 1616 Folio, including the country-house poem 'To Penshurst', the odes 'To Celia' and 'To Heaven', the song 'That Women Are but Men's Shadows', and the epistle 'To Sir Robert Wroth' — the volume that made the estate, the court, and the virtuous life the matter of English lyric.
plot_or_argument: No plot: the poems move from the celebration of Penshurst's hospitality and Sidneyan estate-life, through the songs and odes of love and devotion, to the epistles and epitaphs that map Jonson's moral world of patrons and friends.
narrative_structure: A miscellany of fifteen poems organized by theme — place, love, virtue, mortality — with 'To Penshurst' as its opening masterpiece.
principal_characters: the poet; the Sidney family (at Penshurst); Celia; Sir Robert Wroth; the Countess of Bedford
meter_and_prosody: Couplets, odes, and songs of classical restraint, including the famous lyric 'Drink to me only with thine eyes' (a cento from Philostratus).
historical_context: Collected for the 1616 Folio; 'To Penshurst' (c. 1612) founded the country-house poem that Lanyer, Carew, and Marvell would continue.
literary_significance: Home of the English country-house poem and of Jonson's most enduring lyrics — the classical counterweight to the metaphysical fashion.
bibliographical_notes: First printed in the Folio, 1616. Standard edition: The Cambridge Edition of the Works of Ben Jonson, ed. David Bevington, Martin Butler, and Ian Donaldson (2012).
